items.question: How did you frame your research agenda around applying language models to biology?
items.object: Applying language models to DNA and proteins
items.answer: I really started my career at OpenAI, so I was on the early team there. It was a nonprofit back then, so it was a pretty good time to be there. We did GPT-1, GPT-2, scaling laws. The question was, if the models can learn to speak English, German, French, why can't they learn to speak DNA and protein? That was kind of my research agenda since then.

items.question: How do you understand the advances in protein modeling that made 2024 feel like the right time to start Chai Discovery?
items.object: Advances in protein modeling that made 2024 the right time to start Chai Discovery
items.answer: I think it was a pretty important time, because if you look at the kind of methods that we were bringing in, there's been a lot of these changes on the edges, if you will. But it's all about how do we find the right deep learning architectures with the right compute configuration and the right model architectures? What are the right tasks to apply it to? We're talking about how we even knew that 2024 is the right time to start the company. As Matt was saying, these are all different kinds of amino acid sequences and people thought that antibody class of problem was going to be too hard, and we started to see the first signs of life that actually this was starting to work. I think a lot of it fueled by some of the new architectures we're bringing to the problems. I think it was diffusion models back then. The first time anyone was able to generate reasonable-looking proteins was the advent of diffusion models. It was pretty crazy. There were a bunch of generative modeling approaches that would kind of work if you had a bunch of data. People got these working for images. There were a bunch of tricks to make this better and better along the way. We've definitely borrowed a lot of those ideas in our domain as well.

items.question: Why do you think diffusion models worked so well for generating proteins?
items.answer: Yeah, diffusion is not a one-step process. I think up until this point the main generative design paradigm was called variational autoencoders. In that case you're saying, I want to just compress my input distribution. You have some proteins you want to make look kind of like fuzzy Gaussian vectors. That task is just really hard. Maybe today if we tried super hard I think we'd crack it. But at the time I think it wasn't really developed enough to work for our problems. What turned out working really well was just giving the model more time to think and showing it more examples: here's a slightly broken-looking protein. How do you make it better? You can break that protein more and more and make it look more and more noisy, more and more broken, and teach the model just quick little shortcuts. All right, here's how I make it slightly better. You can just keep asking over and over again: make it slightly better, make it slightly better. Breaking the problem down to that scale worked really well for biology.

items.question: How do you think about the mix of expertise Chai Discovery needs as its models improve?
items.object: Chai Discovery's approach to building its team
items.answer:
We've been really pragmatic about this at Chai. If you look at the founding team, it was mostly AI researchers. People who had worked on either scaling models or getting them to work in this domain. But really with each generation of model, the kind of people we've needed for the next milestone has changed, or I'd say probably has expanded. If you look at Character 2, that's the point when we started to bring in some of the most incredible antibody engineers and scientists in the world. When we hired Andy Young, people asked us if we had pivoted into building a full-stack drug pipeline because they're like, 'You'd be crazy not to do that if Andy joined your team.' I think Andy has enjoyed running more antibody campaigns in the past couple of months than he's probably run in his whole career, which is very cool to see.

As the model started to get better, we needed to build up a product team because while the researchers might get the models to the point that they're very powerful, you need to build the right product interfaces so the models are actually useful. That's where we started to bring on people who have built some of the most exciting products we know about today. Our co-founder Jack worked at Stripe, Monaz who was one of the top 10 code contributors at Stripe, Neil who ran his own cybersecurity company before security started to become very important as we deploy this to our big partners.

As we started to scale up, we brought in people who've really done a lot of the GPU hacking, if you will, in order to scale up our systems so they don't break when we're running them at scale. We had an email from, or a Slack message from, one of our hyperscalers the other day where we had a cluster, I think, that had some issue to it and they're like, 'Oh, the GPUs got too hot. I think you guys are running too many.' And we're like, 'Isn't that the point?'

items.question: Why do you think guiding principles matter when building an open-ended AI research company like Chai?
items.object: Guiding principles for building Chai as an open-ended AI research company
items.answer: I think a lot of the company building process, though, is taking a philosophy and actually sticking with it and iterating on that and just having some guiding principles. When you're building a blue-sky research company, if you will, Chai is almost like one of these neo labs. We have this big AI problem we're going after where, as we make progress on it, that opens up opportunity for our customers. But if you're going to work on something so open-ended that way, you need some principles to guide you. I think we've done a very good job on tracking those principles in the company, working on it.

items.question: Why do you set such a high bar for demonstrating progress with AI models in biology?
items.object: Rigor in evaluating progress with AI models in biology
items.answer: I think being really rigorous is so important in this space. You can fool yourself so easily in biology. The error bars in the wet lab are actually quite large as well. So it's actually a little bit different than if you look at code generation, for instance. If you look at SWE bench, people are like, 'Oh, I got 16% and 17% and 18%.' I mean, in biology if you're plus or minus 5% in your lab, that all might be the same. So it actually just means the bar is really high in terms of the step changes that you want to see with the models, but you also need to be really honest with yourself about whether you're making progress or not. You could come up with some fancy model that looks like it works well on one or two new tasks, but it's very important to show that that works more generally if you're actually trying to build a product that can bring the field forward.

items.question: Why did you choose to build Chai Discovery as infrastructure for the pharmaceutical industry rather than develop your own drug pipeline?
items.object: Chai Discovery's infrastructure and partnership business model
items.answer: Yeah, first of all, I think both of these paths are great and they can create tremendous value. We've always been really excited about building infrastructure for the industry. Our bet when we started, to go back to those results in Matt's house a few years ago, was that this is how most future drugs are going to be discovered. If that's the case, somebody needs to go and build that infrastructure and make it happen. I think part of this too is a lot of our founding team, including Matt and I, had worked in companies before where we had built these full-stack drug pipelines. We were building AI models, we're putting those drugs in the clinic. Again, we're pretty bitter lesson pill as well, and our thinking was as the models get better, we want to be spending more of the money making better models as opposed to diverting those resources into clinical trials and things like that. One of the interesting things about our business model is as the models get better, actually it wins us the right to continue investing more in them. You have partnerships with these pharma companies that are paying off today and allow us to continue investing in it. So it's a much more scalable business in that way. I just think about the ultimate impact that we can create for the world is a lot larger. We've always wanted to just partner broadly with the ecosystem. It goes back to this point about fooling yourself in biology. If you work on a small number of drug targets, you might come up with the most exquisite molecules, creating a ton of value for the world by doing that. But you might miss the forest for the trees because maybe your model doesn't generalize to the other 500 molecules that people are going to make that year. If you partner with people, you just can't fool yourself. Look at our partners, Eli Lilly, Novartis, Organics, Pfizer. These are not companies that take this stuff for granted. You have to really deliver on these partnerships for them to take you seriously. That means it can't just work some of the time. When we ship models at Chai, they really have to work, they have to deliver value to our partners, and it's not like we made some molecule, doesn't fully work, we're going to have our chemists clean it up a little bit. It's almost a harder business to pull off. I think that's one of the reasons why you haven't seen it pursued many times. If you work on a drug pipeline, there might be ways to fix things up later. There will be the proof of what happens in the clinic, of course. But when you have this partnering-based model, you have to be really rigorous about your models. Your models have to work really well because otherwise those partners aren't going to come easily. So it's made our life harder, I think, in many ways, but I think it's also the more rewarding path if we can get it to work.

items.question: How has working with pharmaceutical partners shaped your view of their willingness to adopt AI?
items.answer: Yeah, we went into these partnerships. I think a lot of people told us that pharma doesn't know how to use AI, it's not like a tech-forward industry and things like that. To be honest, that hasn't really been our experience. I think that these are, again, very rigorous partners, very rigorous customers. They're going to test every one of our claims before they start to deploy these things. But when they see the data, they go all in, because pharma is an innovation industry. It's interesting just to think about even the whole economics of the pharma industry. If you build a product in pharma, like a drug, you only have exclusivity on that drug for a certain period of time, and you have to continue to reinvest. Eli Lilly is a trillion-dollar pharma company right now. If they don't get more blockbuster drugs, they will not be a trillion-dollar pharma company forever. I think that forces these companies to really be on their game of adopting new technologies and deploying them and trying to stay ahead. Pharma is a very competitive arena. There's a lot of people trying to bring these drugs to patients. By the way, it's great for patients, but it means that you have to be on top of your game here. Once you're through that door and your models are working, we've seen adoption scale up very quickly and people thinking about how to use the models in incredibly creative ways.

items.question: How do you see Chai Discovery’s partnership model contributing to the long-term improvement of its AI models?
items.object: Chai Discovery’s partnership model and iterative model development
items.answer: I really like the incentive structure that it creates as well, taking more of the partnership model. As our models get better, we get better results to our customers and so on. I think that's a nice side effect for us as well. Chai has been incredibly focused. As the models get better, you can iterate on a better model with better data and so on. A lot of what we see and a lot of what our partners are using the model for, generating binders, antibodies, and so on, we're also doing a lot of dogfooding in-house. We have a whole science team that's using the models and just trying to understand what they can do. A lot of that comes back to, okay, now that we've unlocked use case X, what type of new data can we generate? How can we make the model better that way? Really, that's been the long-term vision of Chai: we never thought, we're going to build this one model that's going to solve all of this. We know that, like in other fields, there are going to be multiple iterations of this model. As you get better and better models, you get this flywheel effect, I guess.

items.question: How do you use model evaluation to keep Chai Discovery advancing at the frontier?
items.object: Chai Discovery's model evaluation and capability development
items.answer: Well, first of all, I think it goes back to looking at the results and not fooling yourself and being rigorous. One of the reasons why we do a lot of evaluation of the models is mainly to hill climb the models itself. I think if you look at many of the capabilities that we've brought in, they've kind of been first in the field. You look at our Chai 2 model, getting to a success rate where you didn't have to do large library screening anymore to see results. A couple months later, showing how we could bring in a lot of these developability properties we've talked about before, like manufacturability of the molecules. In many cases we are pushing the model forward and trying to see these emerge. Then we try to quickly lock those in. How do we make those capabilities even more pronounced so they become production ready and we can ship them to our customers?

items.question: What do you consider the real competitive bar for Chai Discovery's AI drug design models?
items.object: The competitive benchmark for AI drug discovery
items.answer: One of the things I like to tell the team is that it's not like we are head-to-head with other model providers. All of us are working against nature. Nature's actually been a pretty good baseline. People have done drug discovery a certain way for a long time. Matt talked about how maybe you don't want to add module 24 to the Chai model. But people have added module 240 to the existing wet lab protocols. They have been tuned quite considerably. One of the scientists on our team, Andy Young, was one of the first people working on yeast display at MIT, actually two decades ago. He's got 20 years' experience in Pfizer and Genentech, really honing in these methods. Has a drug approval to his name and antibodies. I think you look at someone like that and Andy knows how to make a good antibody with existing tools. That is actually the bar that we need to clear. Now, of course, I think the ceiling on AI is going to be a lot higher than what we've managed to do before. Otherwise, what would be the point of doing this? We didn't start the company just to make a 10 times faster mouse. We started this to make breakthrough medicines that weren't possible before. But ultimately, that is the bar that we needed to clear in order to get adoption. I think we hit that inflection point a couple months ago. That's why you've seen a lot of these big pharma announcements. But now we just need to continue to hone in on making these things even better.

items.question: What do you find most rewarding about the results you're seeing at Chai Discovery?
items.object: The results of Chai Discovery's work
items.answer: I think my favorite part is probably the results. That sounds a bit cliché, but there's nothing like, it's working, right? I think many of us in the company, we've been working in AI for a long time. There's all this experience you built up. To know that you're applying it to something that really matters, even just take Matt and I: we've been working on this problem for 10 years. A couple years ago I'm looking at something like, 'Yeah, we're writing some cool papers. Everyone is celebrating this. Are we actually making the world better? Is this actually going to impact some patients?' I think now the answer is actually yes. We have reached the point where this is going to make a big difference in the world. Every time you get one of these breakthrough results, anytime there's a new feature on the product that makes our customers' lives easier, whenever there's new lab results coming back from the science team, it's always so exhilarating to realize this is actually going to change the world in a pretty profound way.

items.object: Engineering reliability and long-term development speed at Chai Discovery
items.answer: We're running the company and we have real partners that are relying on this. Things have to work. You ship a new model generation. How do you make sure that there's no bugs in that? How do you make sure you don't have regressions? This is no longer just the blue-sky research problem of, 'Oh, we got some cool results and we move on.' We've had to have really high priorities on having production-level code bases. As the team grows, how do we make sure that the code base is in a state that more people can contribute to this? Something that one of our other co-founders, Zach, likes to say is that if you want to move fast in the long term, you sometimes have to just move a little bit slower in the short term. Make sure that you are building something. Again, that goes back to that compounding idea. It goes back to we don't add module 25 to make the next thing work. Sometimes you're so excited to get to the next result and you just want to jump into it, but we have real partners, some of the biggest companies in the world that are now relying on us. It's important that we realize that, take that responsibility to heart, and make sure we're building systems that continue to work.

items.question: Why did you want Chai Discovery to have a simple name?
items.answer: Biotech companies have such complicated names. We wanted something that's going to be much simpler. We're trying to make this whole thing simpler, right? So we need a simple name to go along with it.
quotes: biotech companies have such complicated names. We wanted something that's going to be much simpler. We're trying to make this whole thing simpler, right? So we need a simple name to go along with it.

rubrics.text: The response presents Chai Discovery’s simple name as an expression of its broader aim to make biotechnology simpler.

items.question: Why are you excited about Chai Discovery's deployments with pharmaceutical partners over the next six to twelve months?
items.object: Chai Discovery's deployments with pharmaceutical partners
items.answer: I think for me it's just the deployments that are happening. We've announced a couple of these partnerships and I'm really excited just to hear about the results that our partners are bringing online. It goes back to this point of making a real difference and also why I'm so happy to see how these partnerships are going. As we're working with these folks, the models are not sitting on a shelf somewhere. They're actually being used on real programs. People are trying to approach devastating diseases where, if Chai could give them a molecule that works, it could really change the lives of patients. I'm really excited to see how that goes. The pace of progress here is incredible, but also the pace of the models. A year ago you could not zero-shot a molecule and have a good sense that your program was going to work. Now that's changed. Someone might zero-shot a molecule and be like, 'I think we're going to bring this program to the clinic now.' A year later, they might even have some of those first molecules going into patients. The speed of that is incredible, and sometimes you get some shivers thinking about this stuff. Matt has some patents from our last company about generating the molecule on the computer, and these things are now in patients. Just to think about the scale: I don't know, a few years from now, do we have dozens? Do we have hundreds of Chai molecules going into people? It's a bit mind-blowing to think about what that might look like for patients.
